title: The Labor Day swing band parade that won a film with Louis Armstrong
summary: He combined his band with Les Hite's into a giant swing band for the Labor Day parade, winning the prize and a part in 'Every Day's a Holiday' with Armstrong and Mae West, where he held a trombone.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Yeah. And I did a lot of things with Georgie Stohl, recordings, you know. Then when Louis Armstrong came out there -- in fact, see, every Labor Day they had a union -- they had a parade and every union hired

No, just march. But previous to that they always had marching bands. So I made a proposition with the black union out there -- they had a black union and white union. I said, well, why don't we put together a gigantic swing band and blow in this parade. They said, how you going to do it? I said, well, let me handle it.

So I got Les Hite's band and my band and put them together. Had ten saxophones, ten brass, used four guitar players and two tuba players. And I made an arrangement on "Swing High, Swing Low," and one on "Christopher Columbus." And we rehearsed for two weeks and we went into this parade.
Now, what year is this, '36? Because Christopher Columbus came out in '36?

This might have been '37. This probably was '37. And we marched down Broadway in L.A. and the crowd just followed us all the way to City Hall. And we won this prize. I led the parade with my clarinet, let the band. And we won the prize.
So the pay-off was to make the picture with Louis Armstrong and Mae West, "Every Day's a Holiday." Now, in the picture, Louis MARCHED in front of the band and I was
holding a trombone in the picture. But that's how we got that picture.
Well, that's typical of Hollywood logic, you know. You're a reed player and you're holding a trombone. How'd they figure that out?
Well, that was the only thing for me to do, I guess. Because everything else in the band was filled out. So anyway, that's how we got this picture.

And then after that I -- we played down -- I took my band down -- before that we had taken our band to Santa Monica and played around there. So then after I was working in the studio awhile, it was 1938, I was itching to come back to New York anyway and Fletcher Henderson's band came out.
